Masks created from the template rotated by 0° or 180° were always followed by masks created from the template rotated by 90° or 270°, and vice versa.

In each trial, participants had to press a 'yes' or a 'no' button indicating whether or not they had seen a target letter on the attended side of the screen. The trial ended after a button press, or 5 seconds after the presentation of the third pair of masks. Buttons were pressed with left and right middle fingers and the response mapping was counterbalanced across participants.

Each trial in the experimental part was followed by a screen with two elements: a question "Have you seen this letter?" (black Arial, 22 pt font size) presented against the white background on the top of the screen (centered vertically to the level of 5.65 cm above the fixation cross, and horizontally to the center of the screen); and a black rectangular frame placed on the one side of the fixation cross, indicating which letter the question refers to. The frame was scaled to the size of the mask and centered in the same place as the stimuli on this side of the screen. Below the frame, 4 points of the scale were displayed in a row from left to right together with short versions of the descriptions related to each point of the scale (Arial, 22 pt font size, black, centered vertically to the level of 4.24 cm below the fixation cross and horizontally to the center of the screen with the distance of 10.59 cm between the center of two neighboring points). The first point was described as 'I have not seen anything', the second point as 'I have seen something', the third point as 'I have seen it quite clearly', and the fourth point as 'I have seen it very clearly' (PAS; Ramsøy & Overgaard, 2004).

Participants responded by pressing one of four buttons using their left middle finger for the first point of the scale, left forefinger for the second point, right forefinger for the third point, and right middle finger for the fourth point. Note that responses 1 and 4 were made with the same buttons as 'yes' and 'no' responses during the experimental trials, but the specific correspondence varied across participants. The procedure always waited until the subjective rating response was made. The next trial was presented with a random delay of 0.7-1.3 s.

In the whole experiment 40% of trials contained a target letter (384 trials in total). In half of those trials (192 trials in the procedure), a target letter was presented on the attended side, and accompanied by a distractor presented on the unattended side. In the other half (another 192 trials), a target letter was presented on the unattended side of the screen, with a distractor letter displayed on the attended side. Half of the trials containing a target letter were masked trials (96 trials with the target on the attended side and 96 trials with the target on the unattended side), and the other half were unmasked (96 trials with the target on the attended side and 96 trials with the target on the unattended side). In those unmasked trials, the target letter was always unmasked while the accompanying distractor letter was always masked.

The next category of trials, constituting 40% of all trials (384 trials in total), were those containing two distractor letters presented on both sides of the screen. Half of those trials were masked (192 trials), and in the other half were unmasked (192 trials). Further, in half of the unmasked trials, the unmasked letter was on the one presented on the attended side (96 trials) and in the other half, it was the one displayed on the unattended side (96 trials).

The remaining 20% of all trials were 'catch' trials (192 in total), half of which contained an empty spot (blank) on the attended side of the screen, and a distractor letter on the unattended side (96 trials), and the other half containing a distractor letter on the attended side, and blank on the unattended side (92 trials). Catch trials were always masked.

Note that all trials used in the procedure can be grouped in 10 equinumerous categories.

Five categories can be described as trials containing one of five types of stimuli (i.e. empty screen, masked distractor, masked target, unmasked distractor on unmasked target) on the attended side and a masked distractor on the unattended side of the screen, while the second five categories can be described as trials containing a masked distractor on the attended side and one of those five types of stimuli on the unattended side. The rates of trials of each type were preserved within each subsequent series of 40 trials in experimental blocks as well as in the training block.

In the majority of trials (87,5% of trials, 840 trials in total) the subjective rating of stimulus visibility concerned the letter presented on the attended side of the screen. The exceptions, in which participants had to rate their experience of what was presented on the unattended side were: 24 trials containing a masked target on the unattended side, 24 trials with the unmasked target on the unattended side, 24 trials with masked distractors on both sides of the screen, 24 trials with unmasked distractor on the unattended side, and 24 'catch' trials with an empty spot on the unattended side. Trials with the PAS rating referring to the unattended side of the screen were intermixed randomly within the experimental procedure, in a way that each type of those trials appeared exactly once in each series of 40 trials.

Overall the changes implemented in this experiment with respect to the procedure used by Koivisto and colleagues (2009) involved the shorter presentation duration of letters (8.3 ms instead of 17 ms) and dynamic masking with three masks, instead of two. Furthermore, we decided not to include control trials that were used in the original study, and instead, we introduced catch trials in which only one letter was presented. Finally, participants had to provide a response in the target detection task at each and every trial, and to control the visibility of presented stimuli all trials were followed by the subjective rating task.

Experimental procedure: Experiment 2

In Experiment 2 participants performed the same target detection task as in Experiment 1.

Importantly, here we decided not to use the subjective rating task during the procedure, and instead, we included a survey at the end of the experiment. The procedure consisted of a training block, six experimental blocks, and the final block followed by the survey. Again in each block participants had to focus their attention on this designated side of the screen and indicate the presence of the target letter specified by the instruction. The training block contained 32 trials presented in random order and those trials were not included in the analysis. As in Experiment 1, in the training block the target letter and the side were picked randomly for each participant. In the following six experimental blocks all combinations of target letters ('U', 'T', 'H') and sides participants should focus their attention on (left and right) were used. The order of experimental blocks was randomized across participants. Each of the experimental blocks contained 4 randomly ordered series of 64 trials, which sums up to a total of 1536 trials in the whole experiment. Trials were presented with random trial-to-trial intervals of 0.7-1.3 s and after each series, participants could take a self-paced break. Six experimental blocks were followed by the additional final block of 32 trials, after which participants responded to eight survey questions. In this block target letter and the side to attend were chosen randomly for each participant.

In the present experiment, no catch trials were included, therefore each trial contained either a target letter and a distractor, or two distractors presented on opposite sides of the screen. The placing and timing of letters, as well as the masking procedure were identical to those applied in Experiment 1. In the experimental blocks 25% of trials (384 trials in the procedure), a target letter was presented on the attended side, and accompanied by a distractor presented on the unattended side. In half of those trials the target letter was masked (192 trials) and in the other half this letter was unmasked (192 trials). In the next 25% of trials (384 trials), a target letter was presented on the unattended side of the screen, with a distractor letter displayed on the attended side and again in half of those trials target letter was masked (192 trials) and the other half unmasked (192 trials). In all the trials containing a target letter, the accompanying distractor letter was masked. The remaining 50% of all trials (768 trials in total), contained distractor letters presented on both sides of the screen. In half of those trials, both letters were masked (384 trials), and in the other half, one letter was unmasked (384 trials) with half those trials having an unmasked distractor letter on the attended side (192 trials), and another half, having it the unattended side (192 trials). In summary, all trials used in the procedure can be grouped into 8 equinumerous categories corresponding to the 8 combinations of stimulus type (target or distractor), masking (masked or unmasked), and the side (attended or unattended). The rates of trials of each category were preserved within each subsequent series of 64 trials in experimental blocks as well as in the training block.

In the final block, only unmasked trials were used, with equal number of trials per each combination of stimulus type (target or distractor) and side on which it was presented (attended or unattended). Participants were not warned that this block was any different from the preceding six experimental blocks. After completing the sequence of 32 trials, the presentation of trials stopped and participants were asked to fill out the survey regarding the final block and the whole experiment. The survey started with the question about the quality of the experience of letters appearing on the attended side of the screen during the last block.

Participants responded on the four-point scale inspired by PAS (Ramsøy & Overgaard, 2004).

Possible answers were 'I haven't seen any letters', 'I have seen something but I was not able to recognize letters', 'I have seen unclearly, but was able to recognize letters', and 'I have seen letters very clearly'. Next participants had to answer two 'yes or no' questions about the last block, first they were asked whether they noticed target letters on the unattended side of the screen, and second, whether they had seen any other letters on the unattended side. This was followed by the question about the quality of the experience of letters appearing on the unattended side of the screen in the last block with possible answers the same as in the first question. In the fifth question, participants were asked to rate in what percentage of trials in the last block they had seen any letter. Possible responses were: 'around 25%', 'around 50%', 'around 75%', and '100%'. Note that as all of the trials in the last block were unmasked participants should have seen the letter in 100% of trials. In the last question regarding the final block, we asked participants how often when they had seen the letter, it was presented on the attended or unattended side. Possible responses were: 'only on the attended side', 'more often on the attended side', 'equally often on both sides', and 'more often on the unattended side'. The next two questions in the survey were identical as two previous ones, but concerned the whole experiment, and not just the last block. The possible responses were the same as in the previous two questions. During the survey participants gave their responses by pressing one of four buttons using their left middle finger, left forefinger, right forefinger, and right middle finger respectively. When only two options were possible (in 'yes or no' questions) they could only use a second and third button. The procedure always waited for participants to make a response before moving to the next questions.

Overall Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 with the overall number of experimental trials, lack of the catch trials and visibility ratings, and the addition of the final block followed by the survey.

Behavioral analysis

Analysis of behavioral data was conducted using custom-made Python scripts. Regarding the target detection task, in both experiments, trials with no response provided were excluded from the analysis. This resulted in the median number of trials retained and analyzed trials per participant equal to 959 (range = [932, 960]) in Experiment 1, and to 1568 (range = [1533, 1568]) trials in Experiment 2. The analysis of PAS ratings provided in Experiment 1 was performed on all trials, as the procedure forced participants to rate their experience on the PAS scale in each trial. In each of the experiments, behavioral data collected from all participants were assembled in a long format and fed to the multilevel Bayesian statistical model which accounted for the interindividual variability in response biases.

The results from the survey conducted in Experiment 2 were evaluated qualitatively. One participant failed to finish the survey and responded to only the first five questions, thus only those responses entered the summary of survey results.

EEG recording and analysis

The EEG signal was continuously recorded during the experimental procedure with 64 Ag-AgCl electrically shielded electrodes (Biosemi Active-electrodes) mounted on an elastic cap (Biosemi) and positioned according to the extended 10-20 system. Two referential electrodes (Flat-Type Active-electrodes, BioSemi) were located on the left and right earlobes. HEOG). EEG and EOG signals were then filtered using a band-pass 0.1 Hz to 40 Hz (-6 dB cutoff) zero-phase FIR filter with a Hamming window (filter() method of Raw object in MNE package; Widmann et al., 2015). Next, signal was segmented into 1400 ms-long epochs corresponding to experimental trials, each covering the period from -200 to 1200 ms with respect to the onset of letters. On each channel we applied a baseline correction against the mean voltage during the 200 ms pre-stimulus period and then the signal was resampled to 256 Hz. Finally, we conducted a few last steps in order to remove faulty trials and clean the signal from movement artifacts. First, we rejected no-response trials, which reduced the total number of trials to the median 959 (range = [800, 960]) out of 960 in Experiment 1, and the median 1568 (range = [1544, 1568]) out of 1568 in Experiment 2. Next, we excluded trials in which participants blinked during the presentation of the stimulus or moved their eyes to one of the letters in the time window chosen for ERP analysis. Specifically, we identified epochs with with VEOG maximum peak-to-peak signal amplitude exceeding 140 μV in the -100 -100 ms time window, or HEOG maximum peak-to-peak signal amplitude exceeding 80 μV in the 0 -500 ms time window and removed them from the signal. The remaining oculomotor artifacts were identified in the EEG signal by decomposing it into 64 independent components using Independent Component Analysis (ICA; Makeig et al., 1996), and correlating each component with the HEOG and VEOG channels (using Pearson correlation).

Components contaminated with oculomotor activity were selected using iterating z-scoring, and components whose correlation coefficients exceeded 3 standard deviations from the mean were excluded from the data (find_bad_eogs() method of ICA object in MNE package).

In the last step, we applied a standardized and automatic artifact rejection procedure implemented in the Autoreject package (Jas et al., 2016; 2017). The algorithm first calculates the rejection thresholds individually for each participant and channel (fit() method of the AutoReject object in the Autoreject package; we choose a random search method), next from each epoch it removes channels which exceed the threshold and fills the resulting gaps by interpolating the signal from the neighboring electrodes. Finally, if too many 'bad' channels are discovered in a given epoch, the whole epoch is rejected from the dataset (transform() method of the AutoReject object in the Autoreject package; for details of the procedure see Jas et al., 2016 Jas et al., , 2017)). In Experiment 1, the median number of epochs retained after preprocessing and used in further analysis was 875.5 out of 960 (range = [559, 958]). In Experiment 2, this number was 1485 out of 1568 (range = [1100, 1554]).

ERP analysis

According to the existing literature, VAN should be observed over occipitotemporal scalp regions (Koivisto & Revonsuo, 2010; Pitts et al., 2012; Shafto & Pitts, 2015 , Förster et al., 2020; Dembski et al., 2021; Dellert et al., 2021). Furthermore, VAN is usually be more pronounced in the hemisphere contralateral to stimulus presentation (Koivisto & Grassini, 2016; Eklund & Wiens, 2018; Harris et al., 2020; Doradzińska & Bola; 2024), thus, as all manipulations used in the present study were unilateral (i.e. concerned either attended or unattended side of the visual field, but never both of them at once), we focused our analysis on contralateral sites. Specifically, VAN was analyzed on the left cluster containing P7, PO7, P9, or on the right cluster of following electrodes: P8, PO8, P10. For the selection of temporal windows grand averaged waveforms were created by pooling signals recorded by both clusters of electrodes together and averaging signals across epochs, conditions and subjects (Fig. 2). Based on the visual inspection we have selected the 140-190 ms window for the early VAN (N170 component) and the 190-285 ms window for the late VAN (P2-N2 components). Noteworthy, time windows used in the analysis were defined orthogonally to statistical comparisons between conditions, such as the inflation of the Type I error rate was prevented (Keil et al., 2014).

ERP effects were analyzed using Bayesian hierarchical models. Each subcomponent (early and late VAN) was analyzed separately. For a given time window, we calculated the mean amplitude of the signal in a given time-window and averaged across electrodes in the predefined cluster contralateral to the stimulus presentation. This was done for each epoch separately. In Experiment 1 values obtained for all participants were pooled together into two arrays (representing early and late VAN), each consisting of 16203 data points. The same was done for values obtained in Experiment 2 resulting in two arrays of 28460 data points each.

Data in this form were introduced into the statistical models. Note that for visualization purposes ERP waveforms in each condition were obtained simply by averaging the signal in each time-point across epochs and subjects.

Statistical analysis

All behavioral and ERP effects were statistically evaluated using Bayesian mixed models.

All analyses were conducted in RStudio 1.4.1717 (RStudio Team, 2021), which is an open-source software based on the R programming language (R Core Team, 2021). Models were fitted using the 'brms' package (Bürkner, 2017). Overall we have conducted 3 analyses of behavioral data: of responses in target detection task in Experiment 1, of analogous data collected in Experiment 2, of PAS ratings collected in Experiment 1. Further we pursued four analyses of ERP data, that is early and late VAN amplitudes in each of the experiments separately. For each analysis, to establish a maximal fixed effect structure well suited for our data, we have conducted the iterative reduction of model complexity, starting with the maximal model (containing all considered population-level factors and their interactions), and ending on the simple intercept model, with the maximal random-effect structure fixed across all considered models. Model convergence was verified by checking whether R ̂ parameters for all effects are equal to 1 and only models that successfully converged were considered for further analysis. Obtained models were evaluated using Pareto smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO), implemented in the 'loo' package (Vehtari, et al., 2017) and the final model was picked based on the ELPD (Expected Log Pointwise Predictive Density for a new observation), with the account to the standard error of the estimated ELDP difference of the evaluated model and the best fitting one.

Specifically, we chose the maximal model for which the ELDP distance from the best model did not exceed 2 standard errors. Each of fitted models contained a maximal random effect structure including a random intercept of participants and random slopes of all considered population-level effects and their interactions.

Behavioral responses collected in target detection tasks were analyzed using Bernoulli model with a probit link function and a random intercept of a participant. Priors for all covariates were set to normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 10. In the analysis of data collected in Experiment 1, we considered population-level effects that included a five-level factor of stimulus type (masked catch, masked distractor, masked target, unmasked distractor and unmasked target), a two-level factor of side (attended or unattended), and their interactions. For the analysis of data collected in Experiment 2 fixed effect structure included three two-level factors of: masking (masked or unmasked), stimulus (target or distractor), and side (attended or unattended), as well as their interactions.

PAS ratings collected in Experiment 1 were evaluated using the ordinal model with probit link function, flexible thresholds, and a random intercept of a participant. Priors for the covariates were set to normal distribution with mean 0 standard deviation 10. Considered fixed-effects included a five-level factor of stimulus type (masked catch, masked distractor, masked target, unmasked distractor and unmasked target), a two-level factor of side (attended or unattended), and their interactions.

In both experiments, both ERP effects were investigated using linear Gaussian models with the identity link function. Before the analysis of each component, trials in which ERP amplitude exceeded 3 standard deviations from the mean were excluded from the dataset (less than 0.9% of values). After fitting the intercept model we extracted the sigma parameter and used it to set a normal distribution prior with mean 0 and standard deviation equal to 10 times sigma. Fixed effects considered in analyses of early and late VAN included three two-level factors of: masking (masked or unmasked condition), side (attended or unattended), and stimulus (target or distractor), and their interactions. Catch trials were excluded from the analysis of the ERP signal. In all ERP analyses we checked for the presence or absence of an awareness-related (masking) effect (negative or positive difference between masked and unmasked conditions), and the interactions of this effect with factors of side and stimulus.

Next, we investigated the impact of spatial attention (effect of side) and type of stimulus (effect of stimulus) on the absolute values of ERP waveforms.

For each analysis, we report estimates (M) and 95% credibility intervals (CI) derived from the final model. Furthermore, to conceive the inference about the presence and the direction of effects in our data we performed a non-linear hypothesis testing. We report the evidence ratio for the one-sided hypotheses about the differences between conditions (Evid. Ratio 1 ), and in case of small values (i.e. differences not exceeding 95% CI) also the evidence ratio for two-sided hypotheses of two conditions being equal (Evid. Ratio 0 ). Evidence ratio for a one-sided hypothesis refers to a posterior probability under the hypothesis against its alternative (i.e a one-sided hypothesis in the opposite direction), while for a two-sided (point) hypothesis is an equivalent of a Bayes factor (BF) computed via the Savage-Dickey density ratio method.

Results

Behavioral results Experiment 1

The estimated probabilities of 'target' responses in the target detection task are presented in Figure 3. The model selected for the analysis was the one containing factors of stimulus type and side, and their interaction. Our findings indicate that both masked targets and masked distractors displayed on the attended side resulted in the same probability of 'target' responses as catch trials with no letter presented on the attended visual field (catch: M = 1.27%, CI = [0.67%, 2.23%]; target: M = 1.68%, CI = [0.97%, 2.85%]; distractor: M = 1.25%, CI = [0.69%, 2.22%]; target vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 6.21, Evid. Ratio0 = 58.30; distractor vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 0.93, Evid. Ratio0 = 98.80). Furthermore masked targets displayed in the attended field evoked the same number of 'target' responses as masked distractors (Evid. Ratio1 = 7.52, Evid. Ratio0 = 73.17). The same pattern of results was observed for masked letters presented in the unattended visual field (catch: M = 1.39%, CI = [0.77%, 2.41%]; target: M = 1.07%, CI = [0.56%, 1.92%]; distractor: M = 1.46%, CI = [0.81%, 2.50%]; target vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 0.18, Evid. Ratio0 = 85.24; distractor vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 1.39, Evid. Ratio0 = 145.92; distractor vs target: Evid. Ratio1 = 0.13, Evid. Ratio0 = 99.43). Unmasked targets presented in the attended side were associated with much higher probability of 'target' responses than unmasked distractors presented in the attended side (target: M = 86.94%, CI = [82.69%, 90.55%]; distractor: M = 3.35%, CI = [2.09%, 5.21%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000) as well as than unmasked targets presented on the unattended side (unattended target: M = 2.97%, CI = [1.83%, 4.70%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). Finally, among stimuli presented on the unattended side, unmasked targets resulted in more 'target' responses than unmasked distractors (distractor: M = 1.40%, CI = [0.77%, 2.44%]; Evid. Ratio1 = 2665.67).

The estimated PAS ratings collected in the subjective rating task in Experiment 1 are displayed in Figure 3. The model selected for the analysis was the one containing factors of stimulus type and side, and their interaction. Our results suggest that masked targets presented on the attended side of the screen were associated with the same PAS ratings as catch trials (catch: M = 1.05, CI = [1.03, 1.11]; target: M = 1.07, CI = [1.03, 1.13]; Evid. Ratio1 = 11.62, Evid. Ratio0 = 53.79), however masked distractors displayed on the attended side were related with slightly higher visibility ratings than both catch trials and masked targets (distractor: M = 1.09, CI = [1.05, 1.16]; distractor vs catch: Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000; distractor vs target: Evid. Ratio1 = 185.05). On the unattended side both, masked distractors and masked targets resulted in PAS ratings comparable to ratings of catch trials (catch: M = 1.05, CI = [1.02, 1.11]; target: M = 1.08, CI = [1.04, 1.16]; distractor: M = 1.04, CI = [1.02, 1.10]; distractor vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 0.60, Evid. Ratio0 = 86.91; target vs catch: Evid. Ratio1 = 15.77, Evid. Ratio0 = 32.08), but masked targets were related to slightly higher responses than masked distractors (Evid. Ratio1 = 33.78). Furthermore, our analysis shows that unmasked letters were generally much more visible than masked ones, regardless of their status assigned in the task, and the side of presentation (unmasked attended target: M = 3.39, CI = [3.16, 3.60]; unmasked attended distractor: M = 3.14, CI = [2.86, 3.39]; unmasked unattended target: M = 3.09, CI = [2.80, 3.36]; unmasked unattended distractor: M = 3.03, CI = [2.72, 3.31]; attended target unmasked vs masked: Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000; attended distractor unmasked vs masked: Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000; unattended target unmasked vs masked: Evid. ERP results Experiment 1 ERP waveforms and estimates derived from the model are depicted in Figure 4. In each of the conducted analyses, we first investigated whether VAN is modulated by attention by estimating effects related to awareness (i.e. involving the factor of masking) and interactions of awareness with attention-related factors (side and stimulus). Next, to test whether manipulations of endogenous attention alone can induce a VAN-like effect, we evaluated the influence of side of presentation (side) and the type of stimulus (stimulus) and on the absolute values of ERP waveforms. values in the early (left panel) and late (right panel) VAN time windows with respect to the presentation side (attended or unattended), masking condition, and the type of presented stimulus (target or distractor).

Dots depict estimated values and error bars depict 95% credibility intervals derived from the statistical model. Early VAN In the early time window of VAN, the ERP signal was analyzed with a maximal model containing factors of masking, side, and stimulus as well as all possible interactions. The estimates of the model provide us with substantial evidence that regardless of the side of presentation and the type of stimulus, unmasked, visible letters produced lower values of ERPs when compared to masked, invisible ones (unattended distractor: masked, M = -2.27μV, CI = [-3.45μV, -1.01μV], unmasked, M = -3.21μV, CI = [-4.69μV, -1.73μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 33.63; unattended target: masked, M = -2.37μV, CI = [-3.61μV, -1.12μV], unmasked, M = -3.33μV, CI = [-4.89μV, -1.74μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 25.40; attended distractor: masked, M = -1.88μV, CI = [-3.09μV, -0.64μV], unmasked, M = -3.63μV, CI = [-5.10μV, -2.16μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 3999.00; attended target: masked, M = -1.32μV, CI = [-2.58μV, -0.09μV], unmasked, M = -3.69μV, CI = [-5.19μV, -2.18μV], Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). Further, we found that VAN was modulated by the factor of side, as its amplitude was higher for targets presented in the attended visual field when compared to targets on the unattended side (Evid. Ratio1 = 443.44). However, when investigating the impact of side to VAN evoked by distractors, collected evidence suggest that distractor letters evoked comparable VAN regardless of the side of presentation (Evid. Ratio1 = 17.43, Evid. Ratio0 = 44.67). Finally, we found no interaction between VAN and the type of presented stimulus neither on the attended nor on the unattended side (unattended, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.89, Evid. Ratio0 = 268.08; attended, Evid. Ratio1 = 11.90, Evid. Ratio0 = 63.70). When investigating the effects of side and stimulus on the absolute ERP values we discovered that none of those factors evoked a typical attention-related negative deflection of the registered signal. Specifically, target stimuli evoked generally the same amplitudes as distractors (unattended masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 2.06, Evid. Ratio0 = 347.46; attended masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.04, Evid. Ratio0 = 55.48; unattended unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 1.71, Evid. Ratio0 = 435.05; attended unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 1.41, Evid. Ratio0 = 342.31), and stimuli presented on the unattended side produced comparable amplitudes of ERP component as those presented on the attended side (distractor masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.14, Evid. Ratio0 = 135.00; distractor unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 6.33, Evid. Ratio0 = 158.23; target unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 4.72, Evid. Ratio0 = 247.28). The only exceptions are masked target stimuli, as we found that invisible targets presented on the attended side resulted in more positive ERP values than masked targets presented on the unattended side (Evid. Ratio1 = 1332.33). Noteworthy this effect is counterintuitive, as stimuli presented within the spotlight of attention usually evoke more negative ERP values in the window of the N1 component. Overall our data indicate that early VAN was present regardless of stimulus type and the side of stimulus presentation. The amplitude of VAN was influenced by the side on which the stimulus was presented, but this was true only for target letters. This modulation probably resulted from more positive values of absolute ERP waveform observed for masked targets on the attended side when compared to masked targets on the unattended side. No other attention-related effects were present. Late VAN For the analysis of ERP values in the late time window of VAN, we selected a model containing factors of masking, side, and stimulus, and all two-way interactions (i.e. without the three-way interaction between those factors). Our results indicate that VAN was present for both types of stimuli, presented on both sides of the visual field. Specifically, unmasked letters evoked lower values of ERP potentials than masked ones (unattended distractor: masked, M = 1.17μV, CI = [0.10μV, 2.28μV], unmasked, M = -0.64μV, CI = [-1.92μV, 0.66μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 799.00; unattended target: masked, M = 1.61μV, CI = [0.52μV, 2.71μV], unmasked, M = -0.70μV, CI = [-2.12μV, 0.71μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 7999.00; attended distractor: masked, M = 1.71μV, CI = [0.53μV, 2.93μV], unmasked, M = -0.17μV, CI = [-1.41μV, 1.09μV], Evid. Ratio1 = 1999.00; attended target: masked, M = 2.18μV, CI = [1.01μV, 3.39μV], unmasked, M = -0.19μV, CI = [-1.49μV, 1.14μV], Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). Moreover, the amplitude of VAN was not impacted by the factor of side (Evid. Ratio1 = 1.31, Evid. Ratio0 = 221.23), nor by the type of the stimulus (Evid. Ratio1 = 14.36, Evid. Ratio0 = 80.51). Similarly as in the early time window of VAN, in the late time window, we did not obtain any negative deflections of ERP waveform related to the attentional manipulations. Specifically, the factor of stimulus did not impact ERP waveforms evoked by letters presented on the unattended side (masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.05, Evid. Ratio0 = 18.80; unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 1.30, Evid. Ratio0 = 458.43) and unmasked letters presented on the attended side (Evid. Ratio1 = 1.15, Evid. Ratio0 = 371.16). As for the masked letters presented on the attended side, we actually observed a positive enhancement of ERP values evoked by targets when compared to distractors (Evid. Ratio1 = 30.37). The factor of side also did not have an impact on registered amplitudes (distractor masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.05 Evid. Ratio0 = 62.40; distractor unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.11, Evid. Ratio0 = 130.47; target unmasked. Evid. Ratio1 = 0.11, Evid. Ratio0 = 145.97), with the exception of masked targets, as again they evoked more positive ERP values when presented on the attended side, than when presented on the unattended side (Evid. Ratio1 = 22.53). Therefore as in the case of the early VAN time window, the only observed effects of attention were positive, which is the opposite of what we expected.

In summary, the results obtained for the late VAN indicate that this negative differential component was evoked by unmasked letters regardless of their status for the task, and the side of their presentation. Furthermore, late VAN was not modulated by any attention-related factors. We did not observe VAN-like negativity evoked by attention, and in fact, we obtained evidence for the positive enhancement of ERP waveform in response to masked target letters presented on the attended side of the screen

Behavioral results Experiment 2

The estimates derived from the analysis of responses provided in the target detection task are presented in Figure 3. The model selected for the analysis was the one containing factors of stimulus, masking and side, and all their interactions. We observed that masked targets were related with slightly more probable 'target' responses than masked distractors (target: M = 1.12%, CI = [0.70%, 2.03%]; distractor: M = 0.43%, CI = [0.21%, 0.87%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000), but only when presented on the attended side (target: M = 0.54%, CI = [0.26%, 1.06%]; distractor: M = 0.66%, CI = [0.33%, 1.25%]; Evid. Ratio1 = 0.30, Evid. Ratio0 = 126.41). In unmasked condition target letters presented on the attended side evoked much more 'target' responses than distractors displayed on the attended side (target: M = 87.72%, CI = [83.08%, 91.59%]; distractor: M = 1.25%, CI = [0.70%, 2.22%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000) and than targets presented on the unattended side (unattended target: M = 2.24%, CI = [1.32%, 3.74%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). Finally unmasked targets presented on the unattended side of the screen resulted in more 'target' responses than unmasked distractors presented in the unattended field (distractor: M = 0.73%, CI = [0.37%, 1.37%]; Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000).

These results indicate that unmasked target letters were easily recognized by participants, with the percentage of 'target' responses to targets presented on the attended side oscillating around 87%. The estimated probability of 'target' response for any other type of stimulus was much lower, namely around 1%.

The histograms presenting the distribution of responses in the survey are depicted in Figure 5. Responses suggest that in the final block participants found unmasked letters presented on the attended side of the screen more visible than unmasked letters presented on the unattended side. Importantly, only one participant provided responses indicating that they were not aware of unmasked letters presented on the unattended side of the screen in the final experimental block. Specifically they responded that they have not seen neither the target letter, nor the distractor, and that letters presented on the unattended side were not visible for them. However the same participant responded also that in the main part of the experiment they were aware of presented letters in around 75% of trials, and that visible letters appeared more often on the unattended side of the screen. Overall our results indicate that participants were aware of stimuli presented outside the spotlight of spatial attention. ERP results Experiment 2 ERP waveforms and estimates are depicted on Figure 6. In each of the conducted analyses, we first investigated the interaction between VAN (constituted by the effect of masking) and attention-related factors (side and stimulus), and next we evaluated the influence of the type of stimulus and side of presentation on the absolute values of ERP waveforms.

Early VAN

The model chosen for the analysis of ERP values in the early time window of VAN was the maximal one containing factors of masking, side, and stimulus as well as all possible interactions between them. The investigation of effects related to stimulus visibility provided evidence that early VAN was present for letters presented in the attended visual field Therefore our analysis indicates that in the early time window, VAN was modulated by both the type of stimulus and the side of presentation, to the extent that this differential component was completely absent for distractor letters presented in the unattended visual field. Furthermore, we observed VAN-like negative deflections of the ERP waveform that were elicited by the manipulations of attentional processing of consciously perceived stimuli.

Late VAN

For ERP values in the late time window, the model selected for the analysis was the maximal one including all considered population-level effects (masking, side, and stimulus) Overall we obtained evidence showing that late VAN was present regardless of attentional manipulations, however, its amplitude was modulated by both the type of presented stimulus and the presentation side. Furthermore, both the type of the presented stimulus and the side on which it was displayed influenced the absolute values of ERP, in a way that attentionally salient content evoked a negative deflection of ERP waveform.

Discussion

The aim of the present study was to investigate to what extent Visual Awareness Negativity (VAN) -a differential ERP component proposed to specifically reflect perceptual awareness (for review see: Koivisto & Revonsuo, 2010; Railo et al., 2011; Rutiku & Bachmann, 2017; Förster et al., 2020; Dembski et al., 2021) -is impacted by the mechanisms of spatial and feature-based endogenous attention. We conducted two experiments in which the task-relevance of a stimulus and the location of the spatial attention focus were manipulated orthogonally to the visibility of presented stimuli. In both experiments we found that VAN, understood as the difference between ERP responses to seen and unseen stimuli, was modulated by both feature-based and spatial attention. Specifically, in Experiment 1 both attentional mechanisms were reflected in the amplitude of the early , while the late remained unaffected. In Experiment 2 both attentional processes influenced VAN in both time-windows. In fact, in Experiment 2 the impact of attentional manipulation was so pronounced that the early VAN was completely suppressed for unattended stimuli (namely for distractors presented on the unattended side of the visual field). These results corroborate and complete the outcomes of our previous study (Doradzińska & Bola, 2024) in which we found a pronounced modulation of VAN by exogenous attention related to emotional saliency of presented stimulus and by endogenous feature-based attention. Overall, by showing that VAN's amplitude is substantially modulated by various attentional mechanisms our results indicate that VAN is not a specific correlate of awareness.

Experimental dissociation of attention and awareness

Although awareness and attention seem closely related, a growing body of evidence indicates that they can be dissociated from each other and each of them is realized by a separate neural mechanism (for review see: Tallon-Baudry, 2012; Maier & Tsuchiya, 2021).

Thus in the attempt to distill a genuine NCC one should carefully differentiate neural processes related to awareness from those caused by attentional selection (Aru et al., 2012; de Graaf et al., 2012), but also consider that any manipulation of attention might influence the consciousness itself. Therefore in the present study we collected and analyzed subjective awareness ratings to ensure that our masking procedure was effective and that attentional manipulations did not interfere with the manipulation of stimulus visibility.

In Experiment 1 participants performed a trial-by-trial rating of the subjective visibility of letters presented in different attentional conditions. Obtained results indicated that masked letters were not consciously perceived, while unmasked ones were highly visible, regardless of whether they appeared on the attended (the one on which participants conducted the target detection task) or on the unattended (the opposite one) side of the screen. Importantly, as the subjective rating task sometimes referred to the letters presented on the unattended side of the screen, it is likely that participants were inclined to deploy some attentional resources on that side. This interference of the subjective rating task on spatial attention manipulation may potentially explain the lack of attentional modulation of the late VAN in Experiment 1.

To eliminate this problem, in Experiment 2 the visibility of presented letters was only measured retrospectively, at the end of the experimental procedure. This retrospective measure focused on consciously perceived stimuli and provided evidence that during the whole experiment, participants were aware of unmasked letters appearing on both sides of the visual field, including the unattended side, as none of the participants provided coherent responses suggesting otherwise. Importantly, in Experiment 2 VAN was modulated in both early and late time windows, indicating that the manipulation of attention was more effective than in Experiment 1. Overall our data suggest that in Experiment 1 attention was dissociated from consciousness despite inefficient manipulation of attention, whereas in Experiment 2 we achieved more robust manipulation of attention while maintaining the distinction between effects related to attention and awareness.

Suppression of early VAN and the inattentional blindness problem

A putative NCC should be present always when a stimulus is consciously viewed.

Strikingly, in the present study we obtained a complete suppression of early VAN for distractors presented outside the spatial attention focus. The very similar result was obtained in our recent study (Doradzińska & Bola, 2024) in which we also observed a lack of early VAN for attentionally irrelevant, non-salient images. Importantly, the early subcomponent of VAN was proposed to reflect the elementary, pre-cognitive phenomenal experience and thus to be immune to attentional manipulations (Railo et al., 2011) but our findings undermine this postulate by showing that early VAN is not even necessary for awareness to occur.

Our present work was motivated by results obtained by Koivisto and colleagues (2009), who also found that unmasked letters presented in the unattended visual field do not evoke VAN. Importantly, based on their data, the authors concluded that spatial attention is a prerequisite of consciousness. They referred to the inattentional blindness -a phenomenon where subjective visibility of otherwise easily perceivable images is completely suppressed when attentional resources are directed elsewhere (Simons & Chabris, 1999; Pitts et al., 2012). Specifically they claimed that the suppression of VAN was caused by the suppression of awareness for letters displayed on the unattended side of the screen. However, in their study Koivisto and colleagues (2009) did not include any empirical measure of awareness of unattended stimuli, and thus such interpretation was purely speculative and based on a reverse inference (i.e. they assumed that VAN is a correlate of awareness, thus no VAN meant no awareness). On the contrary, awareness ratings used in our study show that participants were aware of attentionally irrelevant stimuli and thus that the observed lack of VAN is not caused by the suppression of stimulus awareness.

Our findings do not provide strong evidence against the hypothesis that attention is a prerequisite of conscious experience (Dehaene et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2012). Specifically, our procedure did not include a condition in which we could prove that zero attention was paid. What we can show though is that when endogenous attention was to some extent suppressed -for stimuli defined as distractors in the target detection task and presented in a to-be-ignored side of the visual field -unmasked letters were still visible to the participants.

Spatial attention modulates VAN

What constitutes the novelty of this study with respect to the previous one (Doradzińska & Bola, 2024) is that in the present paradigm we included the manipulation of endogenous spatial attention. Our data show that the amplitudes of both early and late VAN highly depend on whether the stimulus is presented within or outside of the internally directed spatial attention focus.

Up to our knowledge the study of Koivisto and colleagues (2009) is the only one that tried to tackle the same research problem. While they also manipulated endogenous spatial attention, their statistical analysis did not include any direct test for the interactions between VAN and spatial attention. Instead of that, they measured the amplitudes of VAN evoked by stimuli presented in the attended and unattended visual fields separately, and found VAN only in the attended condition. Further, the results demonstrated that stimuli presented within spatial attention focus evoked higher amplitudes of VAN in the contralateral hemisphere when compared to the ipsilateral one (although for late VAN this was true only for the right visual field and left hemisphere). Although neither of the reported effects is sufficient to conclude whether spatial attention modulates VAN, we argue that the outcomes of this study suggest the presence of such modulation and thus align well with our results.

Further, in a recently published article by Ciupińska and colleagues (2024) investigated the influence of temporal alerting and spatio-temporal orienting on visual awareness and its neural correlates. Among other effects, authors tested whether the presence of a cue that indicates the location of a following target stimulus can influence the amplitude of VAN (when compared to the cue that does not carry the information about the location).

Importantly, despite using highly sensitive statistical methods, they did not observe such an effect. In our view the discrepancies between these findings and the outcomes of our study result from two premises: first, a very short (500ms) interval between the cue and the stimulus used in the procedure of Ciupińska and colleagues (2024) induced a fast, exogenous spatial attention shift (Posner & Petersen 1990). This phenomenon relates to a very different mechanism than sustained endogenously directed focus of spatial attention evoked in our procedure (Chica et al., 2013). Second, location cues used in the procedure of Ciupińska and colleagues (2024) affect not only attention, but also expectations about the following stimulus. This claim is supported by the fact that stimuli preceded by the location cue evoked generally more positive absolute ERP values in the VAN time-window when compared to stimuli preceded by other types of cues (Ciupińska et al., 2024), which is is a typical effect observed for expected stimuli when compared to unexpected ones (Pazo-Alvarez et al., 2003; Czigler et al., 2007; Astikainen et al., 2008; Stefanics et al., 2015). Therefore, in our view Ciupińska and colleagues (2024) investigated a separate cognitive process and thus their findings do not contradict our conclusions of VAN being modulated by endogenous spatial attention.

Feature-based attention modulates VAN

In our previous study (Doradzińska & Bola, 2024) we found that exogenous attention, triggered by the intrinsic saliency of emotional stimuli, impacted primarily the late part of VAN (in line with Zotto & Pegna, Qiu et al., 2022a , 2022b). Endogenous feature-based attention, induced by defining a stimulus as a target, affected the amplitude of VAN in both early and late time windows. The present study corroborates and extends our previous conclusions (Doradzińska & Bola 2024), showing that even much simpler, emotionally neutral visual stimuli (letters when compared to faces), when defined as a target, evoke higher amplitudes of both early and late VAN.

The literature regarding the impact of endogenous feature-based attention on VAN do not provide clear conclusions (for review see : Förster et al., 2020; Filimonov et al., 2026). We argue that the discrepancies in findings can be vastly explained by variations of methodological approaches. For instance several studies failed to observe a modulation of VAN by endogenous feature-based attention (Koivisto & Revonsuo, 2007; Koivisto et al., 2008; Dellert et al., 2022), but in our view these it is due to insensitive or underpowered statistical analysis (for more detailed discussion see Doradzińska & Bola, 2024). In contrast, in our both studies we used highly sensitive hierarchical models, collected substantial groups of participants (over 80 in total) and accommodated a Bayesian statistical framework to test both the presence and the absence of each effect.

On the other hand, all the studies that directly tested the impact of featured-based attention on VAN and provided evidence for the modulation (in line with our findings; Koivisto et al., 2005 Koivisto et al., , 2009;; Koivisto & Revonsuo, 2008; Pitts et al., 2014) have one common issue that allow for alternative explanation of the observed effect. Namely, in all those studies target detection tasks required participants to provide a response only when they perceived a target, and withhold it in trials in which the target did not appear. Accordingly, there was a close correlation between the target occurrence and the button presses, and thus the effects observed as the interaction between VAN and attentional selection might have been confounded by the motor response. To avoid this issue, we designed the target detection task in a way that a button press was made by participants in every trial which thus excluded this confounding effect. Therefore, our findings not only show that endogenous feature-based attention impacts both early and late VAN, but also that this effect is not induced by the processes related to the response preparation.

Finally our results align well with the outcomes of multiple inattentional blindness studies which showed that task-relevant, attended stimuli evoke more negative ERP values in the VAN time-window (Pitts, et al., 2012; Shafto & Pitts, 2015; Schelonka et al., 2017; Schlossmacher et al., 2020; Dellert et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2023). Inattentional blindness paradigm has an important advantage, namely both seen and unseen stimuli are visually identical, which is not the case in the masking procedure used in our study. One could argue that the presence or absence of a mask could confound our results, however our conclusions regarding VAN are based primarily on the interactions between the effect of masking and attentional manipulations. Further, the main reason to include masking procedure is that it allows to create a full-factorial experimental design that cannot be done in inattentional blindness studies, as they by definition lack an attended yet unconscious condition. Thus, conscious of the downsides of visual masking, we argue that using it in our studies was necessary and did not harm our main findings.

VAN as a correlate of attention -theoretical implications

Of our main interest was whether attention affects VAN defined as a component differentiating aware and unaware, but our results can be also interpreted from the angle of absolute ERP response to attentional manipulation. Specifically, we found that the absolute values of ERP signal in VAN time-window were more negative in response to unmasked targets than to distractors, and to unmasked stimuli presented within the spotlight of spatial attention than to those presented outside. This is in line with our previous findings (Doradzińska & Bola, 2024) as well as with multiple observations that, when compared to waveforms evoked by attentionally irrelevant stimuli, contents prioritized by attention evoke a negative deflection of the ERP waveform very similar to VAN in terms of spatio-temporal characteristic (review: Luck, 2012; Luck & Kappenman, 2013). It has even been shown that VAN-like ERP components can be induced by subliminal attentionally-relevant stimuli (Pegna et al., 2008 (Pegna et al., , 2011;; Axelrod et al., 2015; Zotto & Pegna, 2015; Koivisto & Grassini, 2016; Wójcik et al., 2019; Travis et al., 2019; Bola et al., 2021; Mudrik & Deouell, 2022 Doradzińska & Bola, 2024). This overall indicates that VAN can be dissociated from, and therefore is not specific to awareness, and further support the claim that this component reflects attentional processing instead.

VAN is mainly interpreted in the context of (and considered to provide support for) the Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT; Lamme, 2006 Lamme, , 2010)). According to RPT, the local feedback (recurrent) activity within the ventral stream is the neural mechanism of visual consciousness, and VAN reflects the local recurrent activity at the scalp level (Meyer, 2011; Snyder et al., 2015; Lamme, 2018). Importantly, within RPT consciousness is understood as phenomenal consciousness which, by definition, is independent of the processes related to attentional selection (Lamme, 2004). Therefore, what challenges RPT is that the local feedback activity is involved in a multitude of perceptual and cognitive processes including selective attention (Womelsdorf & Fries, 2007; Moore & Zirnsak, 2017). Furthermore, the ventral stream of visual pathway, activity of which is proposed to generate VAN (Pins & ffytche, 2003; Pourtois et al., 2006; Fahrenfort et al., 2007; Veser et al., 2008; Andersen et al., 2022; Kronemer et al., 2022) plays a crucial role in the mechanism of visual attention (Moran & Desimone, 1985; Chelazzi et al., 1993; Luck et al., 1997; Kastner et al., 1999; McAdams & Maunsell, 1999; Reynolds et al., 2000; Di Russo et al., 2003; Buffalo et al., 2010; Fries, 2015). These findings strongly suggest that VAN might reflect the attentional engagement that usually accompanies conscious perception of presented stimuli, rather than subjective awareness per se. In the context of RPT, it implies that this theoretical framework should either abandon the assumption of the independence between consciousness and attention (Graziano, 2022), which would allow maintaining that VAN is a potential index of awareness; or reject VAN as an NCC and propose another mechanism responsible consciousness, that would not be modulated by the processes related to attentional selection.

Conclusions

Our study provides robust evidence that VAN is modulated and, at its early stages, even gated by spatial and feature-based endogenous attention. Together with results of our previous work (Doradzinska & Bola, 2024), our findings indicate that neural activity observed in the VAN spatiotemporal window is affected by the complex intertwining between various attention-related processes. By showing that VAN can be dissociated from awareness, our work indicates that rather than being a marker of phenomenal experience, the mechanism generating VAN is closely related to attentional prioritization.

The scripts used to run the experimental procedure, behavioral and EEG data and statistical models can be downloaded from OSF repositories (scripts, raw recordings, cleaned and epoched data, and mne.Evoked instances from https://osf.io/46cuq/; behavioral and ERP data in long format, which entered statistical analysis, and statistical models from https://osf.io/t63hw/). The Python and R scripts used for data preprocessing and statistical analysis and a custom Python package containing all used functions can be downloaded from Github (scripts, https://github.com/LucjaDoradzinska/letters_van_prep_scripts; package, https://github.com/Lucja-Doradzinska/erp_exp_ld).

VAN evoked by letters presented within the spotlight of attention was characterized by greater amplitude than VAN evoked by stimuli displayed on the unattended side (distractor, Evid. Ratio1 = 99.00; target, Evid. Ratio1 = 7999.00). The analysis of attention-related effects on the absolute ERP values indicated that both the type of stimulus and side of presentation induced negative deflection of signal resembling VAN. Target stimuli were related to lower ERP values than distractors, however, this effect was absent in the masked condition (unattended masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 1.13, Evid. Ratio0 = 555.34; attended masked, Evid. Ratio1 = 0.51, Evid. Ratio0 = 376.60; unattended unmasked, Evid. Ratio1 = 46.63; attended unmasked, Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). The pattern of effects induced by the side of stimulus presentation was more complex. Specifically, in the masked condition letters displayed in the attended field produced higher ERP values than letters presented on the unattended side (distractor, Evid. Ratio1 = 3999.00; target, Evid. Ratio 1 > 8000). In the unmasked condition, distractors evoked comparable ERP values regardless of the side (Evid. Ratio1 = 3.51, Evid. Ratio0 = 173.58), but targets presented in the attended field resulted in lower ERP values than targets presented in the unattended field (Evid. Ratio1 = 29.65)
